analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting on federal lands and protects old-growth, roadless, and special forest areas from logging.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 103 cosponsors — 101 of them Democrats — but never received a vote in any House committee or on the floor before the 1997–99 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned clearcutting and other even-age logging on all federal forest lands — national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, Indian lands, and military installations — and permanently barred logging and road building in Northwest ancient forests, roadless areas, and dozens of named special areas across 26 states. It also would have let any citizen sue violators, including the federal government itself, with fines of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation. It was referred to three House committees, sent to five subcommittees, and then sat without any vote until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or depends on federal forests: the bill would have protected clean water watersheds, habitat for endangered species, hunting, fishing, and recreation areas, and — per its own findings — jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, and recreation that logging damage had cost. Taxpayers would also have benefited if the bill's finding is right that federal logging programs run at a loss to the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users, recreation towns, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits clearcutting, salvage logging, seed-tree cuts, and shelterwood cuts — all 'even-age' logging — on national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, Indian lands, and military forests, requiring a shift within a year to selection management or ecological restoration.

Bans extractive logging and road construction in Northwest Ancient Forests, roadless areas (5,000 acres or more west of the 100th meridian, 1,500 east), and dozens of named Special Areas in 26 states, from the Tongass in Alaska to the Giant Sequoia lands in California.

Gives ordinary citizens real enforcement power: anyone harmed could sue violators, including the United States, for injunctions and civil penalties of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation, with attorney's fees awarded and the government's sovereign immunity waived.

The bill's findings state that federal logging programs are carried out 'at enormous financial costs' to taxpayers and that destruction of large natural forests has cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding industries.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry would lose access to federal timber: no more clearcutting anywhere on federal land and no logging at all in old-growth, roadless, and special areas. Timber-dependent mill towns and logging communities in the Pacific Northwest and rural national-forest regions would bear adjustment costs, and the bill contained no transition assistance for them. Wood-product consumers could face marginally higher prices as supply shifts to private and foreign sources.

drawbacks.text: The bill offered no transition aid for logging and mill communities that depend on federal timber; a sudden ban on even-age logging and old-growth harvest would have cost jobs in timber towns even if, as the bill's own findings argue, selection logging is more job-intensive per board foot.

The citizen-suit provisions — mandatory penalties of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation, attorney's fees, no notice requirement, and waived sovereign immunity — could have flooded federal land agencies with litigation and tied up forest management in court.

The bill imposed its logging restrictions directly on Indian lands by amending the National Indian Forest Resources Management Act, raising fair objections that tribal nations were being subjected to federal management mandates without their consent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental gains were large and durable — permanent protection for the last unlogged old-growth forests, roadless areas, and watersheds, with citizen enforcement to make the rules real. The costs were real too: reduced federal timber supply and pain for timber-dependent towns, with nothing in the bill to ease that transition, plus a litigation-heavy enforcement design. A well-crafted version would have paired the logging restrictions with worker and community transition assistance and narrower suit provisions. The core protection, though, addressed a resource that the bill's findings said was down to less than 10 percent of its original extent.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and five subcommittees, and none of them ever brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on April 17, 1997 with roughly 54 original cosponsors, including the House Democratic whip and members from across the party's caucuses.
The bill eventually reached 103 cosponsors — 101 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican — about a quarter of the House.

The same day it was introduced, the House referred it to three committees — Agriculture, Resources, and National Security — with the timing of each committee's jurisdiction left to the Speaker to determine.

Within three weeks it was parceled out to five subcommittees and executive comment was requested from the Departments of Agriculture, Interior, and Defense; the last recorded action came on May 8, 1997, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the forests it named still open to logging under existing law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry and federal land agencies came out ahead: no logging restrictions were enacted, so clearcutting and old-growth harvest on national forests and other federal lands continued under the rules in place before the bill. Members who wanted the bill could at least point to their cosponsorship, since it never came to a recorded vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies with access to federal timber

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill; delivered introductory remarks on April 17, 1997.

for.name: 101 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members from timber and non-timber states across the country.

for.name: 1 Independent and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only non-Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and majority of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from April 17, 1997 onward; it went only to a subcommittee and never received a markup or vote in the full committee.

against.name: House Resources and National Security Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the two additional committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond subcommittee referrals after the bill was sent to them on April 17, 1997.

against.name: Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Presided over a referral that split the bill among three committees, any one of which could keep it from advancing, with jurisdictional timing left for the Speaker to determine.

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Federal-lands logging companies and trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on logging federal forests; no industry support for the bill appears in the record, and the bill died without action in the committees that oversee federal timber.

sides.party_line_note: 101 of the bill's 103 cosponsors were Democrats, with just one Independent and one Republican, and the Republican chairs of all three committees of referral never let it reach a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended clearcutting on all federal land and banned logging outright in old-growth, roadless, and special areas, cutting off much of the federal timber supply that logging companies harvest below cost to taxpayers, by the bill's own findings. The industry's interest in continuing federal-lands harvest ran directly against the bill's public protections.

industries.industry: Wood products mills and timber-dependent communities
industries.note: Mills and logging towns dependent on national forest timber would have lost supply with no transition assistance in the bill. Some timber towns also earn income from recreation and fisheries that the bill would have protected.

industries.industry: Recreation, tourism, fishing, and hunting businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings state that destruction of large natural forests has already cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, recreation, and guiding; protecting unlogged forests would preserve the resource these businesses depend on.
